Read a CSV in any Unicode encoding

Source: R/read_text.R
read_csv_utf8.Rd

Reads a CSV (or tab-separated) file saved as UTF-8 (with or without a byte-order mark), UTF-16 or UTF-32, and returns its text as UTF-8. This covers Praat's tables, which Praat saves as UTF-16 whenever any cell is not plain ASCII (for example Chinese token names), and Excel's "CSV UTF-8" and "Unicode Text" formats. The app reads every uploaded CSV this way.

Usage

read_csv_utf8(file, ..., sep = NULL, name = basename(file))

Arguments

file

Path to the file.

...

Passed to utils::read.csv(), e.g. stringsAsFactors, check.names, colClasses, na.strings. Not fileEncoding, encoding or text, which are set here.

sep

Field separator. NULL (default) picks a comma or a tab from the first line, as described in Details.

name

File name to use in messages. Defaults to the file's own name; give the original name when file is a temporary copy, as with a Shiny upload.

Value

A data frame as from utils::read.csv(), with all text (values and column names) in UTF-8. Attribute "encoding" gives the encoding the file was read as (e.g. "UTF-8", "UTF-16BE", "GB18030"), and attribute "encoding_note" a sentence for the user when a code page had to be guessed or bytes that are not UTF-8 were replaced (otherwise it is absent). On failure it stops with an error of class "shinytone_read_error" whose message names the file.

Details

The encoding is found from the byte-order mark, or, without one, from where the zero bytes fall (UTF-16 stores each ASCII character with a zero byte). A file with neither is read as UTF-8. If its text is not valid UTF-8, it was saved in an older 8-bit code page. It is read as Chinese GBK/GB18030 (as Excel on Chinese Windows saves CSVs) or Big5 when most of its other characters are common Chinese characters, punctuation or pinyin in that code page, and as Windows-1252 (Western European) otherwise. Either way the result carries a note, as this is a guess.

A UTF-8 file can also hold a few bytes that are not UTF-8, such as one cell pasted in from a Latin-1 source. When its valid UTF-8 characters far outnumber those bytes and it does not read as Chinese GBK or Big5, it stays UTF-8: only those bytes are replaced, each with U+FFFD (the replacement character), and the note names their lines. This also applies to a file with a UTF-8 byte-order mark.

Zero bytes in a text file, such as the padding a crashed save can leave at its end, are dropped.

The separator is a comma unless the first line has tabs and no commas, as in Praat's "Save as tab-separated file".

Excel workbooks (.xlsx, .xls), other binary files, empty files and UTF-16 files with broken characters are refused with an error that says what to do, rather than read in part.

Examples

# A UTF-16LE file with a byte-order mark, as Excel's "Unicode Text" writes
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
txt <- "token,f0\nma1,210\nma2,180\n"
writeBin(c(as.raw(c(0xFF, 0xFE)),
           iconv(txt, "UTF-8", "UTF-16LE", toRaw = TRUE)[[1]]), f)
df <- read_csv_utf8(f)
df
#>   token  f0
#> 1   ma1 210
#> 2   ma2 180
attr(df, "encoding")
#> [1] "UTF-16LE"
